data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The 'strictly more total internal redundancy' of the large service is effectively neutralized for correlated failure if the decentralization is empirically achieved via hardware/software diversity, because a large service operates under a single deployment philosophy that becomes a single point of correlated failure (e.g., a uniform CI/CD pipeline or a uniform firmware version). Thus, the small services' independence of operation\u2014lacking a shared brain\u2014is the dominant factor in surviving shared causes.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the large service can be shown to possess operational independence of redundant components equivalent to the decentralization (e.g., separate teams, disjoint software stacks, disjoint supply chains), the claim weakens.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the decentralized network converges on a single shared implementation (e.g., all small operators use the same cloud provider or the same open-source library), the dominant factor disappears and the large service's planned redundancy wins.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Centralized redundancy is planned: it eliminates independent failure modes by design but also eliminates independent *survival* modes. A single shared cause (e.g., a bad configuration push, a common supply-chain compromise) propagates through the large service's redundant components precisely because they are not independent of each other in operation. A decentralized network has no single point of operational control; even if components are individually less reliable, the probability that a shared cause reaches all of them is bounded by the probability of coincident operational alignment, which is lower than the near-certainty of alignment inside a single large service.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
